bottom_line: In MEGA, diet plus 10–20 mg pravastatin daily reduced coronary heart disease versus diet alone (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.49–0.91).
implications: These data support that, in this trial population, adding pravastatin to diet lowered the incidence of coronary heart disease versus diet alone (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.49–0.91; 66 vs 101 events). The trial does not show a statistically significant reduction in stroke at end of study (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.57–1.21) or total mortality (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.51–1.01). Safety conclusions are limited to the reported finding of no between-group difference in malignant neoplasms or other serious adverse events.

major_points.text: Prospective randomised, open-labelled trial with blinded endpoint assessment in Japanese patients with hypercholesterolaemia and no prior coronary heart disease or stroke.
major_points.quote: Methods In this prospective, randomised, open-labelled, blinded study, patients with hypercholesterolaemia (total cholesterol 5·69–6·98 mmol/L) and no history of coronary heart disease or stroke were randomly assigned diet or diet plus 10–20 mg pravastatin daily.

major_points.text: Primary endpoint was first occurrence of coronary heart disease.
major_points.quote: The primary endpoint was the ﬁrst occurrence of coronary heart disease.
Statistical analyses were done by intention to treat.

major_points.text: Participants randomised: 3966 to diet and 3866 to diet plus pravastatin; mean follow-up 5.3 years.
major_points.quote: Findings 3966 patients were randomly assigned to the diet group and 3866 to the diet plus pravastatin group. Mean follow-up was 5·3 years.

major_points.text: Coronary heart disease events were lower with diet plus pravastatin (66) than diet alone (101), HR 0.67 (95% CI 0.49–0.91).
major_points.quote: Coronary heart disease was signiﬁcantly lower in the diet plus pravastatin group than in the diet alone group (66 events vs 101 events; HR 0·67, 95% CI 0·49–0·91; p=0·01).

major_points.text: No difference reported in malignant neoplasms or other serious adverse events between groups.
major_points.quote: There was no diﬀerence in the incidence of malignant neoplasms or other serious adverse events between the two groups.

guidelines_referenced.text: National Cholesterol Education Program step I diet
guidelines_referenced.quote: Patients in both groups were counselled to follow the National Cholesterol Education Program step I diet.15

criticisms.text: At 5 years, the trial continued for an additional 5 years to increase number of events (extension may affect interpretation vs originally scheduled period).
criticisms.quote: The follow-up period was initially scheduled for 5 years; however, on the basis of recommendations from the data and safety monitoring committee, the study was continued for an additional 5 years to increase the number of events.

criticisms.text: Possibility that the 5-year stroke result could have been due to chance.
criticisms.quote: However, for stroke, the possibility of a chance outcome cannot be ruled out.

criticisms.text: High statin uptake in the diet-only group after 5 years could bias intention-to-treat results toward more conservative outcomes.
criticisms.quote: The high uptake rate after 5 years for statin use in those assigned diet only could have resulted in more conservative outcomes in this intention-to-treat analysis.

criticisms.text: Reasons for the observed risk reduction despite smaller lipid reductions and lower dose were unclear and require further examination.
criticisms.quote: The reasons for this unexpected risk reduction, despite a dose of pravastatin that is half the dose administered to western patients, are unclear and require further examination.

criticisms.text: Risk reduction was low in the LDL <4.01 mmol/L subgroup; further analysis is necessary.
criticisms.quote: However, risk reduction in the subgroup of individuals with LDL-cholesterol concentrations of less than 4·01 mmol/L was low in the present study, so further analysis is necessary
